name: Unit 1 — AP Psychology — Biological Bases of Behavior: The Brain

cards.back: The transmission of genetic information from biological parents to offspring.
Inherited biological and genetic influences on traits, behavior, and development.
Environmental influences and experiences that shape traits, behavior, and development.
An inherited likelihood of developing certain traits or conditions.
The view that psychological traits and behaviors evolved because they helped survival or reproduction.
The process in which traits better suited to the environment are more likely to be passed on.
The belief that human genetics should be 'improved' by controlling reproduction; historically tied to discriminatory practices.
Studies comparing identical and fraternal twins to estimate genetic and environmental influences.
Studies comparing relatives to examine how genetics and shared environment relate to traits.
Studies comparing adopted people with biological and adoptive families to separate genetic and environmental influences.
The brain and spinal cord; the body's main information-processing and control center.
All nerves outside the brain and spinal cord that connect the body with the CNS.
The PNS division that automatically controls involuntary body functions.
The autonomic branch that activates the body's fight-or-flight response.
The autonomic branch that calms the body and restores it after stress.
The PNS division that controls voluntary movement and carries sensory information to the CNS.
Specialized nerve cells that transmit electrical and chemical signals.
Support cells that protect, nourish, and insulate neurons.
A neural pathway that produces a rapid automatic response without conscious thought.
Neurons that carry sensory information from receptors to the CNS.
Neurons that carry commands from the CNS to muscles, glands, or organs.
CNS neurons that relay signals between sensory and motor neurons.
The process by which neurons communicate using electrical and chemical signals.
A brief electrical impulse that travels along a neuron's axon.
Once threshold is reached, a neuron fires a full-strength action potential; below threshold it does not fire.
The action-potential phase when the inside of a neuron becomes less negative as positive ions enter.
The brief reset period after an action potential when the neuron cannot immediately fire again.
The stable negative electrical charge of a neuron when it is not firing.
The reabsorption of released neurotransmitters by the presynaptic neuron.
The minimum level of stimulation needed to trigger an action potential.
An autoimmune disease in which the immune system damages myelin in the central nervous system.
An autoimmune disorder that disrupts acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, weakening muscle activation.
Neurotransmitters that make the postsynaptic neuron more likely to fire an action potential.
Neurotransmitters that make the postsynaptic neuron less likely to fire an action potential.
A neurotransmitter involved in reward, pleasure, motivation, mood, and movement.
A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep, appetite, and stress regulation.
A neurotransmitter and hormone involved in arousal, attention, alertness, and the stress response.
The primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS; important for learning, memory, and plasticity.
The primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS; it reduces neural activity and promotes calm.
Natural pain-relieving and mood-enhancing neurotransmitters released during pain, stress, or intense activity.
A neurotransmitter involved in transmitting and amplifying pain signals.
A neurotransmitter important for muscle contraction, learning, and memory.
Chemical messengers made by endocrine glands that travel through the bloodstream to regulate body processes and behavior.
The 'master gland' at the base of the brain that helps regulate hormone release throughout the body.
A hormone and neurotransmitter that prepares the body for fight-or-flight during stress or danger.
A hormone released mainly by fat cells that signals satiety and helps suppress appetite.
A hormone produced mainly by the stomach that increases hunger and appetite.
A hormone that helps regulate circadian rhythms and the sleep-wake cycle.
A hormone and neurotransmitter involved in social bonding, trust, and attachment.
The oldest, most basic brain region; controls vital functions and links the brain with the spinal cord.
A brainstem structure that regulates vital automatic functions such as breathing, heartbeat, and blood pressure.
A brainstem network that regulates arousal, attention, consciousness, and wakefulness.
A network of brain structures that processes pleasure and reinforces rewarding behaviors.
A structure at the back of the brain that coordinates movement, balance, posture, and learned motor skills.
The brain's outer layer, responsible for higher-level functions such as thinking, perception, and decision-making.
A group of brain structures involved in emotion, memory, and motivation.
A sensory relay station that directs most incoming sensory information to the appropriate cortex areas.
A small brain structure that maintains homeostasis by regulating hunger, thirst, temperature, and sleep-wake cycles.
A temporal-lobe structure important for forming and consolidating new memories.
An almond-shaped structure involved in emotion, especially fear, aggression, and threat detection.
The thick band of nerve fibers connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
The lobes at the back of the brain that primarily process visual information.
The side lobes involved in hearing, language comprehension, and memory formation.
The upper lobes involved in spatial awareness, numerical processing, and body sensations.
Cortical areas that integrate information from different senses and support higher cognitive functions.
A parietal-lobe region that processes touch, pressure, temperature, pain, and body sensations.
The front lobes involved in planning, decision-making, problem-solving, impulse control, and personality.
The mental processes used to understand and produce language.
Complex thinking such as reasoning, planning, problem-solving, and decision-making.
Mental processes used to plan, organize, focus attention, regulate emotions, and manage behavior and time.
A frontal-lobe region central to executive functions such as planning, judgment, decision-making, and self-control.
A frontal-lobe region that plans, controls, and executes voluntary body movements.
Research on people whose corpus callosum was severed, revealing specialized functions of the two hemispheres.
A neurological disorder involving recurrent seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
The idea that the left and right hemispheres are specialized for different functions.
A usually left-frontal brain region important for speech production and grammatical language.
A usually left-temporal brain region important for understanding spoken and written language.
Language impairment from brain damage: Broca's aphasia disrupts fluent speech production; Wernicke's aphasia disrupts comprehension and meaningful speech.
The organization in which each brain hemisphere mainly controls and processes the opposite side of the body.
The brain's ability to reorganize and adapt through experience, learning, or recovery from damage.
A noninvasive method that records the brain's electrical activity using electrodes on the scalp.
A brain-imaging method that estimates activity by measuring changes in blood flow and oxygen levels.
A research method that studies brain function by intentionally damaging a specific brain area, usually in experimental animals.
A measure of how much variation in a trait within a population is associated with genetic differences.
Chemical messengers released by neurons that cross synapses and influence other cells.
The central part of a neuron that contains the nucleus.
Branch-like neuron structures that receive incoming signals.
The long neuron projection that carries electrical impulses away from the cell body.
A fatty insulating layer around many axons that speeds neural transmission.
The junction where one neuron communicates with another cell.
The ends of an axon that release neurotransmitters to communicate with other cells.
A language disorder marked by slow, effortful, nonfluent speech after damage to Broca's area.
A language disorder marked by poor comprehension and fluent but often meaningless speech after damage to Wernicke's area.
Brain tissue rich in neuron cell bodies where much neural processing occurs.
Brain tissue made largely of myelinated axons that connect different brain regions.
